scenes.text: So, how do flexibility, strength and skill training differ? Start with a puzzle. A netball coach spends every session on shooting drills from fixed spots. For eight weeks, training shooting percentage rises steadily. In matches, it doesn't move at all. Write down two reasons the improvement didn't carry over, and one change you'd make to the drill.

All four stretching methods increase range, but they differ in how, in risk, and above all in when. Static stretching moves to mild tension and holds, about fifteen to thirty seconds. It's safe and builds long-term range, but long holds just before explosive work can briefly reduce power. Dynamic stretching moves a joint under control through its range, getting faster and wider. It warms the tissue and rehearses the movement, so it belongs in the warm-up.

Ballistic stretching uses bouncing momentum to push past normal range. It carries the highest injury risk, so it's rarely used, and only by trained athletes whose sport needs fast end-range movement. PNF means stretching, then contracting the stretched muscle against resistance, then relaxing and stretching further, usually with a partner. It's generally the most effective for range, but it's slow and uncomfortable. So, dynamic before, static or PNF after. Timing matters at least as much as the sport.

Last time, load, reps, sets and rest decided whether you build strength, size or power. Equipment decides what else comes with it. Free weights, like barbells and dumbbells, make the athlete stabilise the load, so supporting muscles and balance get trained too, and they transfer well to sport. But they need coaching. Fixed weights, machines, guide the movement path, so they isolate a muscle and are safe without a spotter, good for beginners and rehab, but they transfer less. Body weight needs no equipment, and you make it harder through leverage, range or speed, but it's hard to load heavily. Elastics are different. A dumbbell's load is roughly constant, but a band's resistance rises as it stretches. So the load is greatest near the end of the range, which is often where the joint is strongest. That makes bands useful for rehab and speed work, though the load is hard to measure.

Now the hook. A shot from a fixed spot isn't the same task as a shot in a match. The match adds a decision, an opponent, fatigue and consequence. In Year 11 you saw that practice which looks worse in training often works better in games. Drills repeat a skill in simplified conditions, often with no opponent. They give lots of repetitions and suit new skills or fixing a fault, but they remove the decision. A modified game is a real game with one rule, space, player number or score changed, so the target behaviour becomes the way to win. Want support play in touch football? Two points for a try within three passes. It makes the target situation happen far more often, with the pressure still on. A game for a specific outcome makes one tactical goal the object of play, so players discover the solution. That needs the skills to exist already. So drills build the skill, and games build the decision that selects it.

One question governs all three. Does the improvement show up in the sport? That's transfer. More hamstring range on a mat is worth little to a hurdler unless it's there at speed. A bigger leg-press number doesn't guarantee a faster first step. And a fixed-spot shooting percentage measures a task the match never asks for. The principle underneath is specificity, coming up next: the closer training is to the real task, the more carries over. But it's a spectrum, and both ends cost something. All-specific training gives little variety and few chances to fix a weakness. All-general training builds abilities that never show up on game day. Good programs use both, and know which is which.

Use the same routine. A gymnast needs extreme range under control, so PNF and static work, plus body-weight strength through that full range. The cost is a partner and time, and range needs strength to be safe. A rugby forward needs force in an unstable, contested position, so free weights, with bands for shoulder and hip health. That needs real coaching, because heavy lifting done badly injures. And a junior team with good technique but poor choices has a decision problem, so modified games and games for outcomes, accepting fewer repetitions each. So no method is best. Match it to the demand, and name the cost.
Two things to remember. Dynamic before, static or PNF after. And drills build the skill, games build the decision.

Two exam questions. First. A fourteen-year-old is starting resistance training at school, with a teacher supervising but no spotter. A sprinter wants hip strength near full extension, training alone in a hotel room. For each, choose a way to apply resistance, justify it, and give one limitation. Pause here to answer.

The fourteen-year-old suits body weight and fixed weights, because a guided path is safe without a spotter, with a teacher supervising. The limitation is less transfer to sport. The sprinter suits elastics: portable, with the load rising toward full hip extension, where the sprint needs it. The limitation is that the load is hard to measure. The classic mistake is heavy free weights with nobody watching.

Second. A junior hockey team all dribble well in drills, but in matches they keep dribbling into defenders instead of passing. Design a modified game for them, explain why it works, and name one thing it gives up compared with drills. Pause here to answer.

One option: small-sided games in a narrow grid where a player may take only three touches, or a goal counts double after three passes. The rule makes passing the way to win, while defenders and decisions stay in. It gives up repetitions of technique per player. The classic mistake is running more dribbling drills.

So with every method, ask how it's done, when it belongs, what it costs, and whether it transfers. Now put all five families into a real program and run it for six weeks. At first it works, then the improvement line flattens. Why does a program stop working?
